entries.literal: the Director of Music and the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices led her up to the imperial seat, the curtains were raised, and the music ceased.

entries.zh: 文武三品以上入，《舒和》樂作；
entries.en: Civil and military officials of the third rank and above entered; the music Shuhe sounded;
entries.literal: Civil and military officials of the third rank and above entered; the music Shuhe sounded;

entries.zh: 至位，樂止。
entries.en: when they reached their places, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when he reached his place, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 皇帝入門，《雍和》樂作；
entries.en: The emperor entered the gate; the music Yonghe sounded;
entries.literal: The emperor entered the gate; the music Yonghe sounded;

entries.zh: 至殿前位，樂止。
entries.en: when he reached his place before the hall, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when he reached his place before the hall, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 宰相押冊，皇帝隨冊，樂作；
entries.en: The chief minister escorted the document of investiture, the emperor followed the register, and music sounded;
entries.literal: The chief minister escorted the register, the emperor followed the register, music sounded;

entries.zh: 至殿前置冊於案，樂止。
entries.en: when the document was set on the table before the hall, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when the register was placed on the table before the hall, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 翰林學士、大將軍舁冊，樂作；
entries.en: Hanlin academicians and the grand general bore the register, music sounded;
entries.literal: Hanlin academicians and the grand general bore the register, music sounded;

entries.zh: 置御坐前，樂止。
entries.en: when it was set before the throne, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when it was set before the imperial seat, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 丞相上殿，樂作；
entries.en: The chief counselor ascended the hall, music sounded;
entries.literal: The chief counselor ascended the hall, music sounded;

entries.zh: 至讀冊位，樂止。
entries.en: when he reached the place for reading the register, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when he reached the place for reading the register, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 皇帝下殿，樂作；
entries.en: The emperor descended from the hall, music sounded;
entries.literal: The emperor descended from the hall, music sounded;

entries.zh: 至位，樂止。
entries.en: when he reached his place, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when he reached his place, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 太后宣答訖，樂作；
entries.en: When the empress dowager had finished her proclamation and response, music sounded;
entries.literal: When the empress dowager had finished her proclamation and response, music sounded;

entries.zh: 皇帝至西閣，樂止。
entries.en: when the emperor reached the west side chamber, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when the emperor reached the west side chamber, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 親王、丞相上殿，樂作；
entries.en: Princes and the chief counselor ascended the hall, music sounded;
entries.literal: Princes and the chief counselor ascended the hall, music sounded;

entries.zh: 退班出，樂止。
entries.en: when they withdrew from the ranks and departed, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when they withdrew from the ranks and departed, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 下簾，樂作；
entries.en: The curtains were lowered, music sounded;
entries.literal: The curtains were lowered, music sounded;

entries.zh: 皇太后入內，樂止。
entries.en: when the empress dowager entered the inner quarters, the music ceased.
entries.literal: when the empress dowager entered the inner quarters, the music ceased.

entries.zh: 聖宗統和元年，冊承天皇太后，童子弟子隊樂引太后輦至金鑾門。
entries.en: In the first year of Tonghe, when Emperor Shengzong invested Empress Dowager Chengtian, the boy-disciple musical corps escorted the empress dowager’s carriage with music to the Golden Phoenix Gate.
entries.literal: In the first year of Tonghe, Emperor Shengzong, at the investiture of Empress Dowager Chengtian, the boy-disciple corps music led the empress dowager's carriage to the Golden Phoenix Gate.

entries.zh: 十二律用周黍尺九寸管，空徑三分為本。
entries.en: The twelve pitch pipes were based on the Zhou millet-measure: a nine-inch tube with an inner diameter of three fen.
entries.literal: The twelve pitch pipes used the Zhou millet-measure nine-inch tube, with an empty diameter of three fen as the standard.

entries.zh: 道宗大康中，詔行黍所定升斗，嘗定律矣。
entries.en: In the Dakang era of Emperor Daozong, an edict ordered the adoption of the bushel and peck defined by the millet measure, and the pitch standard was once fixed accordingly.
entries.literal: In the Dakang era of Emperor Daozong, an edict ordered the use of the bushel and peck fixed by the millet measure, and pitch was once regulated.

entries.zh: 其法大抵用古律焉。
entries.en: The method employed was largely that of the ancient pitch pipes.
entries.literal: Its method largely employed the ancient pitch standard.

entries.zh: 大樂
entries.en: Great Music
entries.literal: Great Music

entries.zh: 自漢以來，因秦、楚之聲置樂府。
entries.en: From the Han dynasty onward, a Music Bureau was established to preserve the sounds of Qin and Chu.
entries.literal: From Han onward, on the basis of Qin and Chu sounds the Music Bureau was established.

entries.zh: 至隋高祖詔求知音者，鄭譯得西域蘇祗婆七旦之聲，求合七音八十四調之說，由是雅俗之樂，皆此聲矣。
entries.en: When Sui Gaozu issued an edict seeking masters of music, Zheng Yi obtained from the Western Regions the seven-mode system of the Kuchean musician Sujiva and sought to align it with the theory of seven tones and eighty-four modes; from that point, both court ritual and popular music drew on these sounds.
entries.literal: By the time of Sui Gaozu's edict seeking those who knew music, Zheng Yi obtained from the Western Regions the seven-mode sounds of Kuchean Sujiva, seeking to match the theory of seven tones and eighty-four modes; henceforth ritual and popular music alike were all this sound.

entries.zh: 用之朝廷，別於雅樂者，謂之大樂。
entries.en: What was used at court and distinguished from ritual music was called great music.
entries.literal: Used at court, distinct from ritual music, it was called great music.

entries.zh: 晉高祖使馮道、劉煦冊應天太后、太宗皇帝，其聲器、工官與法駕，同歸於遼。
entries.en: When Jin Gaozu sent Feng Dao and Liu Xu to invest Empress Dowager Yingtian and Emperor Taizong, the musical instruments, musicians, and imperial regalia all passed into Liao hands together.
entries.literal: Jin Gaozu sent Feng Dao and Liu Xu to invest Empress Dowager Yingtian and Emperor Taizong; their musical instruments, artisan officials, and imperial regalia all passed together to the Liao.

entries.zh: 殷人作靡靡之樂，其聲往而不反，流為鄭、衛之聲。
entries.en: The Yin made decadent music whose sound went out and did not return, eventually flowing into the music of Zheng and Wei.
entries.literal: The people of Yin made decadent music; its sound went forth and did not return, flowing into the sounds of Zheng and Wei.

entries.zh: 秦、漢之間，秦、楚聲作，鄭、衛浸亡。
entries.en: Between the Qin and Han dynasties, Qin and Chu sounds arose while Zheng and Wei music gradually died out.
entries.literal: Between Qin and Han, Qin and Chu sounds arose, and Zheng and Wei gradually perished.

entries.zh: 漢武帝以李延年典樂府，稍用西涼之聲。
entries.en: Emperor Wu of Han placed Li Yannian in charge of the Music Bureau and gradually introduced sounds from Western Liang.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu of Han put Li Yannian in charge of the Music Bureau and gradually used Western Liang sounds.

entries.zh: 今之散樂，俳優、歌舞雜進，往往漢樂府之遺聲。
entries.en: Present-day miscellaneous music, with actors, songs, and dances presented in succession, often preserves sounds handed down from the Han Music Bureau.
entries.literal: Today's miscellaneous music, with actors, song, and dance entering in mixture, is often the surviving sound of the Han Music Bureau.

entries.zh: 晉天福三年，遣劉句以伶官來歸，遼有散樂，蓋由此矣。
entries.en: In the third year of Tianfu, Jin sent Liu Gou back with court entertainers; the Liao acquired miscellaneous music, presumably from this event.
entries.literal: In the third year of Tianfu of Jin, Liu Gou was sent with entertainers to return; the Liao had miscellaneous music—presumably from this.

entries.zh: 雜戲：自齊景公用倡優侏儒，至漢武帝設魚龍曼延之戲，後漢有繩舞、自刳之伎，杜佑以為多幻術，皆出西域。
entries.en: Miscellaneous entertainments: from Duke Jing of Qi's actors and dwarfs to Emperor Wu of Han's fish-dragon pageant, and in Later Han rope dances and self-disemboweling acts—Du You regarded most of these as illusion arts originating in the Western Regions.
entries.literal: Miscellaneous entertainments: from Duke Jing of Qi's use of actors and dwarfs, to Emperor Wu of Han's fish-dragon spreading play, Later Han had rope dance and self-disemboweling acts—Du You considered most of these illusion arts, all coming from the Western Regions.

entries.zh: 哇俚不經，故不具述。
entries.en: They are vulgar and unorthodox, and so are not described in full.
entries.literal: vulgar and unorthodox, therefore not fully described.

entries.zh: 鼓吹樂
entries.en: Drum-and-Wind Music
entries.literal: Drum-and-wind Music

entries.zh: 遼太祖奮自朔方，太宗繼誌述事，以成其業。
entries.en: Emperor Taizu of Liao rose to power from the northern frontier, and Emperor Taizong continued his purpose and consolidated his achievements, bringing the enterprise to completion.
entries.literal: The Liao Taizu exerted himself from the northern frontier; Taizong carried on his will and recorded his deeds, thereby completing the enterprise.

entries.zh: 於是舉渤海，立敬瑭，破重貴，盡致周、秦、兩漢、隋、唐文物之遺餘而居有之。
entries.en: He then subjugated Bohai, installed Shi Jingtang, defeated Shi Chonggui, and gathered into his possession the surviving regalia and artifacts of Zhou, Qin, both Han dynasties, Sui, and Tang.
entries.literal: Thereupon he raised up Bohai, enthroned Jingtang, defeated Chonggui, and fully gathered the surviving cultural relics of Zhou, Qin, the two Han dynasties, Sui, and Tang and took possession of them.

entries.zh: 路車法物以隆等威，金符玉璽以布號令。
entries.en: He employed state chariots and ritual regalia to enhance hierarchical grandeur, and gold tallies and jade seals to promulgate his commands.
entries.literal: State chariots and ritual objects to elevate rank and majesty; gold tallies and jade seals to issue commands.

entries.zh: 是以傳至九主二百餘年，豈獨以兵革之利，士馬之強哉！
entries.en: The dynasty endured through nine rulers over more than two centuries—surely this was not due to military advantage and cavalry strength alone!
entries.literal: Thus the succession passed through nine rulers for more than two hundred years—was it solely by the advantage of arms and the strength of men and horses!

entries.zh: 文謂之儀，武謂之衛，足以成一代之規模矣。
entries.en: Civil affairs were called ceremonial protocol and military affairs ceremonial guard—together they sufficed to establish the institutional framework of an entire dynasty.
entries.literal: What is civil is called ceremony; what is martial is called guard—sufficient to form the model of an age.

entries.zh: 考遼所有輿服、符璽、儀仗，作《儀衛志》。
entries.en: Surveying the Liao's chariots and attire, seals and tallies, and ceremonial regalia, I have compiled the Treatise on Ceremonial Guards.
entries.literal: Examining all chariots, attire, tallies, seals, and ceremonial regalia of the Liao, I compose the "Treatise on Ceremonial Guards."

entries.zh: 玉輅，祀天、祭地、享宗廟、朝賀、納後用之。
entries.en: Jade chariot—used for sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, offerings in the ancestral temple, court audiences of congratulation, and receiving the empress.
entries.literal: Jade chariot: used for sacrificing to Heaven, sacrificing to Earth, offering in the ancestral temple, court congratulations, and receiving the empress.

entries.zh: 青質，玉飾，黃屋，左纛。
entries.en: Green body, jade fittings, yellow canopy, and the great banner mounted on the left.
entries.literal: Green material, jade ornament, yellow canopy, great banner on the left.

entries.zh: 十二鑾在衡，二鈴在軾。
entries.en: Twelve pennon pendants on the crossbar and two bells on the handrail.
entries.literal: Twelve pennons on the crossbar, two bells on the chariot rail.

entries.zh: 龍辀左建旂，十二遊，皆畫升龍，長曳地。
entries.en: On the left of the dragon-shaft pole a banner is raised; twelve streamers, each painted with ascending dragons, trail to the ground.
entries.literal: On the dragon-shaft carriage pole a banner is erected on the left; twelve tassels, all painted with ascending dragons, trail long to the ground.

entries.zh: 駕蒼龍，金摐，鏤錫，鞶纓十二就。
entries.en: Drawn by grey-green horses with golden fittings, carved tin ornaments, and twelve sets of braided trappings.
entries.literal: Drawn by blue-green horses, golden bustle, carved tin, twelve sets of braided caparison.

entries.zh: 遼國《勘箭儀》，皇帝乘玉輅至內門。
entries.en: In the Liao Arrow-Verification Rite, the emperor rides the jade chariot to the inner gate.
entries.literal: In the Liao "Arrow-Verification Rite," the emperor rides the jade chariot to the inner gate.

entries.zh: 聖宗開泰十年，上升玉輅自內三門入萬壽殿，進七廟御容酒。
entries.en: In Kaitai 10 of Emperor Shengzong's reign, he mounted the jade chariot, entered the Hall of Ten Thousand Longevities through the inner triple gates, and presented wine before the imperial portraits in the seven ancestral shrines.
entries.literal: In the tenth year of Emperor Shengzong's Kaitai era, ascending the jade chariot he entered the Hall of Ten Thousand Longevities from the inner triple gates and presented wine before the imperial portraits of the seven temples.

entries.zh: 平頭輦，常行用之。
entries.en: Flat-Top palanquin—used for everyday travel.
entries.literal: Flat-Top palanquin: used for ordinary travel.

entries.zh: 制如逍遙，無屋。
entries.en: Of the same design as the Leisure palanquin but without a canopy structure.
entries.literal: The form like the Leisure palanquin but without a canopy house.

entries.zh: 冊承天皇太后儀，皇太后乘平頭輦。
entries.en: In the Rite of Enthroning the Empress Dowager Who Received Heaven, the empress dowager rides the Flat-Top palanquin.
entries.literal: In the rite of enthroning the Empress Dowager Who Received Heaven, the empress dowager rides the Flat-Top palanquin.

entries.zh: 步輦，聖宗統和三年，駐蹕土河，乘步輦聽政。
entries.en: Hand-borne palanquin—in Tonghe 3 of Emperor Shengzong's reign, while encamped at the Tuh River, he conducted state business from a hand palanquin.
entries.literal: Hand palanquin: in the third year of Emperor Shengzong's Tonghe era, encamped at the Tuh River, he rode the hand palanquin to attend to government.

entries.zh: 漢輿
entries.en: Han Chariots
entries.literal: Han chariots

entries.zh: 太宗皇帝會同元年，晉使馮道、劉煦等備車輅法物，上皇帝、皇太后尊號冊禮。
entries.en: In the first year of Emperor Taizong's Huitong reign, Later Jin envoys Feng Dao, Liu Xu, and others furnished chariots, ritual regalia, and court insignia for the enthronement ceremony conferring honorific titles on the emperor and empress dowager.
entries.literal: In the first year of Emperor Taizong's Huitong era, Jin envoys Feng Dao, Liu Xu, and others prepared chariots, ritual regalia, and court insignia to conduct the enthronement rite conferring honorific titles upon the emperor and empress dowager.

entries.zh: 自此天子車服昉見於遼。
entries.en: From this time forward, the Son of Heaven's chariots and regalia first appeared at the Liao court.
entries.literal: From this point the Son of Heaven's chariots and attire first appeared in Liao.

entries.zh: 太平中行漢冊禮，乘黃令陳車輅，尚輦奉御陳輿輦。
entries.en: During the Taiping Enthronement Rite, the Bearer-of-the Yellow presented the ritual chariots, and the Chief Palanquin Attendant presented the palanquins.
entries.literal: During the Taiping enthronement rite, the Bearer-of-Yellow presented the chariots and the Chief Palanquin Attendant presented the palanquins.

entries.zh: 盛唐輦輅，盡在遼廷矣。
entries.en: The palanquins and chariots of flourishing Tang were all held in the Liao court.
entries.literal: The palanquins and chariots of flourishing Tang were all in the Liao court.

entries.zh: 輦：用人挽，本宮中所乘。
entries.en: Palanquin—man-drawn; originally used for travel within the palace.
entries.literal: Palanquin: drawn by men; originally used within the palace.

entries.zh: 唐高宗始制七輦。
entries.en: Emperor Gaozong of Tang first established the seven palanquins.
entries.literal: Tang Gaozong first instituted seven palanquins.

entries.zh: 《周官》巾車有輦，以人組輓之。
entries.en: The Rites of Zhou assigns palanquins to the Chief Carriage Officer, drawn by teams of men.
entries.literal: The "Rites of Zhou" Chief Carriage Officer has palanquins, drawn by men in teams.

entries.zh: 太平冊禮，皇帝御輦。
entries.en: In the Taiping Enthronement Rite, the emperor takes the palanquin.
entries.literal: In the Taiping enthronement rite, the emperor mounts the palanquin.

entries.zh: 儀衛誌一
entries.en: Ceremonial Guards, Part 1
entries.literal: Ceremonial Guards, Part 1

entries.zh: 上古之人，網罟禽獸，食肉衣皮，以儷鹿韋掩前後，謂之鞸。
entries.en: In high antiquity, people hunted game with nets, ate meat and wore hides, and covered themselves front and back with paired deer hides—this was called the bian apron.
entries.literal: The people of high antiquity caught beasts with nets, ate meat and wore hides, covering front and back with paired deer leather—called bian.

entries.zh: 然後夏葛冬裘之制興焉。
entries.en: Only then did the custom of ramie in summer and furs in winter take shape.
entries.literal: Thereafter the system of summer ramie and winter fur arose.

entries.zh: 周公陳王業，《七月》之詩，至於一日於貉，三月條桑，八月載績，公私之用由是出矣。
entries.en: The Duke of Zhou set forth the royal enterprise, and in the "Seventh Month" ode one finds a day spent hunting badgers, the third month devoted to tending mulberry, and the eighth month bearing home the spun cloth—thus arose what supplied both public and private needs.
entries.literal: The Duke of Zhou expounded the royal enterprise; the "Seventh Month" poem goes so far as one day hunting badgers, third month trimming mulberry, eighth month carrying the spun work—public and private uses issued from this.

entries.zh: 契丹轉居薦草之間，去邃古之風猶未遠也。
entries.en: The Khitan roamed among saltwort pastures, and customs of the deep past were still close at hand.
entries.literal: The Khitan moved about among saltwort grass; they were still not far from deep-ancient customs.

entries.zh: 太祖仲父述瀾，以遙輦氏於越之官，占居潢河沃壤，始置城邑，為樹藝、桑麻、組織之教，有遼王業之隆，其亦肇跡於此乎！
entries.en: Emperor Taizu's uncle Shulü, who held the office of yuyue in the Yaonian clan, settled on the fertile banks of the Huang River, founded the first walled towns, and introduced agriculture, sericulture, and weaving. The grandeur of the Liao royal enterprise may well have begun here.
entries.literal: Taizu's father's younger brother Shulü, holding the Yaonian clan office of yuyue, occupied the fertile banks of the Huang River, first established walled settlements, and instituted instruction in planting, mulberry and hemp, and weaving—the rise of the Liao royal enterprise perhaps also took its first traces here!

entries.zh: 太祖帝北方，太宗制中國，紫銀之鼠，羅綺之篚，麇載而至。
entries.en: Emperor Taizu reigned over the north, and Emperor Taizong governed China; purple-silver sable and baskets of gauze and brocade arrived in train upon train.
entries.literal: Taizu became emperor of the north; Taizong ruled China. Purple-silver sable, baskets of gauze and silk—loads arrived in abundance.

entries.zh: 纖麗耎毳，被土綢木。
entries.en: Fine, lustrous, and soft furs spread over the land as silk might cover trees.
entries.literal: Fine, beautiful, soft furs covered the land like silk over trees.

entries.zh: 於是定衣冠之制，北班國制，南班漢制，各從其便焉。
entries.en: Regulations for caps and robes were then established: the northern court followed Khitan national dress and the southern court Chinese dress, each according to its own usage.
entries.literal: Thereupon hat-and-robe regulations were fixed: the northern bureau used national dress, the southern bureau Han dress—each following what was convenient.

entries.zh: 詳國服以著厥始雲。
entries.en: National dress is described in detail here to record how it began.
entries.literal: National dress is set forth in detail to record its beginnings.

entries.zh: 朝服：太祖丙寅歲即皇帝位，朝服衷甲，以備非常。
entries.en: Court dress: when Emperor Taizu took the throne in the bingyin year, he wore court robes over hidden armor as a precaution against emergencies.
entries.literal: Court dress: in the bingyin year Taizu ascended the throne; court dress was worn over armor within, to guard against the unexpected.

entries.zh: 其後行瑟瑟禮、大射柳，即此服。
entries.en: Thereafter this was the dress worn for the sese rite and the great willow-shooting ceremony.
entries.literal: Thereafter, when performing the sese rite and great willow-shooting, this was the dress worn.

entries.zh: 聖宗統和元年冊承天皇太后，給三品以上用漢法服，三品以下用大射柳之服。
entries.en: In the first year of Tonghe, when Emperor Shengzong invested Empress Dowager Chengtian, officials of third rank and above received Chinese court robes and those below third rank the great willow-shooting dress.
entries.literal: In the first year of Tonghe, when Shengzong invested Empress Dowager Chengtian, officials of third rank and above were given Han-style court robes, and those below third rank the great willow-shooting dress.

entries.zh: 皇帝幅巾，擐甲戎裝，以貂鼠或鵝項、鴨頭為扞腰。
entries.en: The emperor wore a wrapped headcloth and martial armor, with sable, goose-neck, or duck-head pieces as waist guards.
entries.literal: The emperor wore a wrapped headcloth and donned armor in martial dress, using sable or goose-neck or duck-head pieces as waist guards.

entries.zh: 蕃漢諸司使以上並戎裝，衣皆左衽，黑綠色。
entries.en: Khitan and Han commissioners of the various bureaus and above all wore martial dress with left-lapped garments in black-green.
entries.literal: Khitan and Han commissioners of the various bureaus and above all wore martial dress; garments were all left-lapped, black-green in color.

entries.zh: 吊服：太祖叛弟剌哥等降，素服受之。
entries.en: Mourning dress: when Emperor Taizu's rebel younger brother Cige and others surrendered, he received them in plain white dress.
entries.literal: Mourning dress: when Taizu's rebel younger brother Cige and others surrendered, he received them in plain white dress.

entries.zh: 素服，乘赭白馬。
entries.en: He wore plain white dress and rode a reddish-white horse.
entries.literal: Plain white dress, riding a reddish-white horse.

entries.zh: 朝服：乾亨五年，聖宗冊承天太后，給三品以上法服。
entries.en: Court dress: in the fifth year of Qianheng, when Emperor Shengzong invested Empress Dowager Chengtian, officials of third rank and above received formal court robes.
entries.literal: Court dress: in the fifth year of Qianheng, when Shengzong invested Empress Dowager Chengtian, officials of third rank and above were given court robes.

entries.zh: 《雜禮》，冊承天太后儀，侍中就席解劍脫履。
entries.en: In the Miscellaneous Rites, at the investiture of Empress Dowager Chengtian, the attendant-in-chief took his seat, removed his sword, and took off his shoes.
entries.literal: In the "Miscellaneous Rites," for the investiture of Empress Dowager Chengtian, the attendant-in-chief took his seat, removed his sword, and took off his shoes.

entries.zh: 重熙五年尊號冊禮，皇帝服龍袞，北南臣僚並朝服，蓋遼制。
entries.en: At the honorific-title investiture in the fifth year of Chongxi, the emperor wore dragon regalia and officials of both northern and southern courts wore court dress—this was Liao practice.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Chongxi, at the honorific-title investiture, the emperor wore dragon regalia; northern and southern officials all wore court dress—this was Liao custom.

entries.zh: 會同中，太后、北面臣僚國服；
entries.en: During the Huitong period, the empress dowager and northern-court officials wore Khitan national dress;
entries.literal: During Huitong, the empress dowager and northern-bureau officials wore national dress;

entries.zh: 皇帝、南面臣僚漢服。
entries.en: while the emperor and southern-court officials wore Chinese dress.
entries.literal: the emperor and southern-bureau officials wore Han dress.

entries.zh: 乾亨以後，大禮雖北面三品以上亦用漢服；
entries.en: After Qianheng, even at great rites northern-court officials of third rank and above wore Chinese dress;
entries.literal: After Qianheng, even for great rites northern-bureau officials of third rank and above also used Han dress;

entries.zh: 重熙以後，大禮並漢服矣。
entries.en: After Chongxi, great rites were conducted entirely in Chinese dress.
entries.literal: After Chongxi, great rites were entirely in Han dress.

entries.zh: 常朝仍遵會同之制。
entries.en: Ordinary court audiences still followed the Huitong regulations.
entries.literal: Ordinary court audiences still followed the Huitong regulations.

entries.zh: 公服：謂之「展裹」，著紫。
entries.en: Official dress, called "zhan guo," was worn in purple.
entries.literal: Official dress: called "zhan guo," worn in purple.

entries.zh: 興宗重熙二十二年，詔八房族巾幘。
entries.en: In the twenty-second year of Chongxi, Emperor Xingzong ordered the eight house clans to wear headcloths and caps.
entries.literal: In the twenty-second year of Chongxi, Xingzong ordered the eight house clans to wear headcloths and caps.

entries.zh: 道宗清寧元年，詔非勛戚之後及夷離堇副使並承應有職事人，不帶巾。
entries.en: In the first year of Qingning, Emperor Daozong decreed that only descendants of meritorious families, deputy yilijin, and attendants holding official posts might wear the headcloth.
entries.literal: In the first year of Qingning, Daozong ordered that those who were not descendants of meritorious kin, nor deputy yilijin, nor attendants with official duties, were not to wear the headcloth.

entries.zh: 儀衛誌二 ○國服
entries.en: Ceremonial Guards, Part 2 — National Dress
entries.literal: Ceremonial Guards, Part 2 ○ National Dress

entries.zh: 遙輦氏之世，受印於回鶻。
entries.en: In the era of the Yaonian clan, the Khitan received seals from the Uighurs.
entries.literal: In the age of the Yaonian clan, they received seals from the Uighurs.

entries.zh: 至耶瀾可汗請印於唐，武宗始賜「奉國契丹印」。
entries.en: Under Khan Yelang, when a seal was requested from Tang, Emperor Wuzong first granted the "Khitan Seal of Service to the State."
entries.literal: When Yelang Khan requested a seal from Tang, Emperor Wuzong first bestowed the "Khitan Seal of Service to the State."

entries.zh: 太祖神冊元年，梁幽州刺史來歸，詔賜印綬。
entries.en: In the first year of the Shence era (916), when the prefect of Youzhou in Liang came to submit, an edict bestowed a seal and investiture cord.
entries.literal: In the first year of Shence, when the military governor of Youzhou in Liang came to submit, an edict bestowed a seal and cord.

entries.zh: 是時，太祖受位遙輦十年矣。
entries.en: By then Emperor Taizu had already held the Yaonian throne for ten years.
entries.literal: At that time, Emperor Taizu had already held the Yaonian throne for ten years.

entries.zh: 會同九年，太宗伐晉，末帝表上傳國寶一、金印三，天子符瑞於是歸遼。
entries.en: In the ninth year of the Huitong era (946), when Emperor Taizong campaigned against Jin, the last Jin emperor presented by memorial one imperial transmission seal and three gold seals, and the Son of Heaven's talismans and regalia then passed to Liao.
entries.literal: In the ninth year of Huitong, Emperor Taizong campaigned against Jin; the last emperor presented by memorial one transmission seal and three gold seals, and the Son of Heaven's talismans and treasures then passed to Liao.

entries.zh: 自大賀氏八部用兵，則合契而動，不過刻木為牉合。
entries.en: From the days of the Greater He clan's eight divisions, armies moved only when the tally halves were joined—nothing more elaborate than carved wooden pieces made to fit together.
entries.literal: From the time of the Greater He clan's eight divisions, when troops were deployed they joined tallies to move—nothing more than carving wood into matching halves.

entries.zh: 太祖受命，易以金魚。
entries.en: After Emperor Taizu received Heaven's mandate, wooden tallies gave way to golden fish tokens.
entries.literal: When Emperor Taizu received the mandate, they were replaced with golden fish.

entries.zh: 傳國寶，秦始皇作，用藍玉，螭紐，六面，其正面文「受命於天，既壽永昌」，魚鳥篆，子嬰以上漢高祖。
entries.en: The imperial jade seal of dynastic transmission was fashioned by the First Emperor of Qin from blue jade, with a chilong knob and six faces. On its front was inscribed, "Having received the mandate from Heaven, may you enjoy long life and enduring prosperity," in fish-and-bird seal script. Ziying of Qin surrendered it to Emperor Gaozu of Han.
entries.literal: The transmission-of-the-realm treasure, made by the First Emperor of Qin, used blue jade, a chilong knob, six faces; its front face bore the text "Ordered by Heaven, long life and eternal prosperity" in fish-and-bird seal script; Ziying presented it to Emperor Gaozu of Han.

entries.zh: 王莽篡漢，平皇后投璽殿階，螭角微玷。
entries.en: When Wang Mang seized the Han throne, Empress Ping hurled the seal down the palace steps, chipping the chilong horn slightly.
entries.literal: Wang Mang usurped Han; Empress Ping cast the seal down the palace steps, and the chilong horn was slightly chipped.

entries.zh: 獻帝失之，孫堅得於井中，傳至孫權，以歸於魏。
entries.en: Emperor Xian lost possession of it; Sun Jian recovered it from a well. It passed down to Sun Quan, who in turn surrendered it to Wei.
entries.literal: Emperor Xian lost it; Sun Jian obtained it from a well; it passed to Sun Quan and was returned to Wei.

entries.zh: 魏文帝隸刻肩際曰「大魏受漢傳國之寶」。
entries.en: Emperor Wen of Wei had clerical script carved along the shoulder reading, "Great Wei receives the Han imperial transmission seal."
entries.literal: Emperor Wen of Wei carved in clerical script on the shoulder area: "Great Wei receives Han's transmission-of-the-realm treasure."

entries.zh: 唐更名「受命寶」。
entries.en: The Tang renamed it the "Seal of Received Mandate."
entries.literal: Tang renamed it "Treasure of Mandate Received."

entries.zh: 晉亡歸遼。
entries.en: When Later Jin collapsed, the seal passed to the Liao.
entries.literal: When Later Jin perished it passed to Liao.

entries.zh: 自三國以來，僭偽諸國往往模擬私制，歷代府庫所藏不一，莫辨真偽。
entries.en: From the Three Kingdoms onward, rival regimes frequently forged their own imitations in private. What successive dynastic treasuries kept varied so widely that none could tell the genuine seal from the copies.
entries.literal: Since the Three Kingdoms, usurping states often privately forged copies in imitation; what successive treasuries held differed, and none could distinguish true from false.

entries.zh: 聖宗開泰十年，馳驛取石晉所上玉璽於中京。
entries.en: In the tenth year of the Kaotai era (1021), during the reign of Emperor Shengzong, an express courier was sent to retrieve the jade seal that Later Jin had surrendered, which was kept at Zhongjing.
entries.literal: In the tenth year of Kaotai under Emperor Shengzong, urgent relay was dispatched to fetch the jade seal presented by Later Jin from Zhongjing.

entries.zh: 興宗重熙七年，以《有傳國寶者為正統賦》試進士。
entries.en: In the seventh year of the Chongxi era (1038), during the reign of Emperor Xingzong, candidates for the presented-scholar degree were tested with the essay topic, "Whoever Holds the Imperial Transmission Seal Holds Legitimate Rule."
entries.literal: In the seventh year of Chongxi under Emperor Xingzong, presented scholars were examined on the essay "He Who Possesses the Transmission Seal Is the Orthodox Succession."

entries.zh: 天祚保大二年，遺傳國璽於桑乾河。
entries.en: In the second year of the Baoda era (1122), the last Liao emperor Tianzuo lost the imperial transmission seal in the Sanggan River.
entries.literal: In the second year of Baoda under Tianzuo, the transmission imperial seal was lost in the Sanggan River.

entries.zh: 杓窊印，杓窊，鷙鳥之總名，以為印紐，取疾速之義。
entries.en: The diaowa seal took its knob from the diaowa, a general term for birds of prey, signifying speed and urgency.
entries.literal: The diaowa seal: diaowa is the general name for fierce birds, used as the seal knob, taking the meaning of swiftness.

entries.zh: 行軍詔賜將帥用之。
entries.en: It was used when edicts on campaign were bestowed upon generals.
entries.literal: Used when campaign edicts were granted to commanders.

entries.zh: 道宗賜耶律仁先鷹紐印，即此。
entries.en: When Emperor Daozong granted Yelü Renxian a seal with an eagle knob, it was of this kind.
entries.literal: When Emperor Daozong granted Yelü Renxian an eagle-knob seal, it was this type.

entries.zh: 符契
entries.en: Tally Tokens
entries.literal: Tally tokens

entries.zh: 儀衛誌三
entries.en: Ceremonial Guards, Part Three
entries.literal: Ceremonial Guards Treatise, Part Three

entries.en: (Seals and Imprints)
entries.literal: (Seals and Imprints)

entries.zh: 王通氏言，舜歲遍四嶽，民不告勞，營衛省、征求寡耳。
entries.en: Wang Tong observed that even when Emperor Shun toured the four sacred peaks every year, the people did not complain of exhaustion, because his camp guards were few and his levies light.
entries.literal: Master Wang Tong said: Shun each year visited all four sacred peaks, yet the people did not complain of fatigue—camp guards were few and requisitions light.

entries.zh: 遼太祖匹馬一麾，斥地萬里，經營四方，未嘗寧居，所至樂從，用此道也。
entries.en: Emperor Taizu of Liao, with a single horse and one command, extended his domain ten thousand li and toured the four quarters without ever settling in one place; wherever he went, people gladly followed—he employed this same principle.
entries.literal: Liao's Taizu, with a single horse and one command, extended territory ten thousand li, managed the four quarters, never dwelt at ease; wherever he went people gladly followed—he employed this same principle.

entries.zh: 太宗兼制中國，秦皇、漢武之儀文日至，後嗣因之。
entries.en: Emperor Taizong also ruled China, and each day brought more of the ceremonial protocol of the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han; his successors followed suit.
entries.literal: Taizong also ruled China; the ceremonial protocol of the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han arrived day by day, and later heirs followed it.

entries.zh: 旄頭豹尾，馳驅五京之間，終歲勤動，轍跡相尋。
entries.en: With yak-tail banners and leopard-tail insignia, they raced among the Five Capitals, laboring throughout the year so that wagon ruts followed one upon another.
entries.literal: With yak-tail banners and leopard-tail insignia, they raced among the Five Capitals; the whole year was labor and movement, wagon ruts following one upon another.

entries.zh: 民勞財匱，此之故歟！
entries.en: The people grew weary and the treasury ran dry—was this not the cause?
entries.literal: The people grew weary and coffers empty—is this not the cause!

entries.zh: 遼自大賀氏摩會受唐鼓纛之賜，是為國仗。
entries.en: From the time Mohe of the Dahe clan received Tang's gift of drums and banners, this became the Liao national regalia.
entries.literal: Liao, from the time Mohe of the Dahe clan received Tang's gift of drums and banners, took this as national paraphernalia.

entries.zh: 其制甚簡，太宗伐唐、晉以前，所用皆是物也。
entries.en: Its regulations were quite simple; before Emperor Taizong's campaigns against Tang and Jin, everything used was of this sort.
entries.literal: Its regulations were quite simple; before Taizong's campaigns against Tang and Jin, everything used was of this sort.

entries.zh: 著於篇首以見艱難創業之主，豈必厚衛其身雲。
entries.en: It is placed at the head of the chapter to show a founder who toiled through hardship to build the realm—not one who necessarily sought lavish personal protection.
entries.literal: It is placed at the head of the chapter to show a founder who toiled through hardship to build the realm—not one who necessarily sought lavish personal protection.

entries.zh: 遙輦末主遺制，迎十二神纛、天子旗鼓置太祖帳前。
entries.en: Under the bequeathed regulations of the Yaonian late ruler, the twelve spirit banners and the Son of Heaven's flags and drums were welcomed and placed before Emperor Taizu's tent.
entries.literal: By the bequeathed regulations of the Yaonian late ruler, the twelve spirit banners and the Son of Heaven's flags and drums were welcomed and placed before Taizu's tent.

entries.zh: 諸弟剌哥等叛，勻德實縱火焚行宮，皇后命曷古魯救之，止得天子旗鼓。
entries.en: When the younger brothers Cige and others rebelled, Jundeshi set fire and burned the traveling palace; the empress ordered Hegulu to rescue the regalia, but only the Son of Heaven's flags and drums were recovered.
entries.literal: When the younger brothers Cige and others rebelled, Jundeshi set fire and burned the traveling palace; the empress ordered Hegulu to rescue them, but only the Son of Heaven's flags and drums were recovered.

entries.zh: 太宗即位，置旗鼓、神纛於殿前。
entries.en: When Emperor Taizong succeeded to the throne, he placed the flags, drums, and spirit banners before the hall.
entries.literal: When Taizong succeeded to the throne, he placed the flags, drums, and spirit banners before the hall.

entries.zh: 聖宗以輕車儀衛拜帝山。
entries.en: Emperor Shengzong, with a light chariot and ceremonial guard, paid homage at Di Mountain.
entries.literal: Emperor Shengzong, with a light chariot and ceremonial guard, paid homage at Di Mountain.

entries.zh: 大賀失活入朝於唐，娑固兄弟繼之，尚主封王，飫觀上國。
entries.en: Da He Shihuo attended court at Tang; the Suogu brothers succeeded him, married imperial princesses and were enfeoffed as kings, and feasted their eyes on the splendors of the Tang court.
entries.literal: Da He Shihuo entered court at Tang; the Suogu brothers succeeded him, married imperial princesses and were enfeoffed as kings, and feasted their eyes on the superior realm.

entries.zh: 開元東封，邵固扈從，又覽太平之盛。
entries.en: At the Kaiyuan eastern feng sacrifice, Shaogu followed in attendance and again beheld the grandeur of the High Tang.
entries.literal: At the Kaiyuan eastern feng sacrifice, Shaogu followed in attendance and again beheld the grandeur of the Great Peace era.

entries.zh: 自是朝貢歲至於唐。
entries.en: From then on, tribute missions arrived at Tang every year.
entries.literal: From then on tribute missions came yearly to Tang.

entries.zh: 遼始祖涅裏立遙輦氏，世為國相，目見耳聞，歆企帝王之容輝有年矣。
entries.en: The founding ancestor of Liao, Nieli, established the Yaonian clan and served for generations as chief minister of state; through what he saw and heard, he had long admired and yearned for the splendor of the Tang emperors.
entries.literal: Liao's founding ancestor Nieli established the Yaonian clan, generation after generation serving as chief minister of state; by eye and ear he had long admired and yearned for the emperor's splendor.

entries.zh: 遙輦致鼓纛於太祖帳前，曾何足以副其雄心霸氣之所睥睨哉！
entries.en: When the Yaonian clan presented drums and banners before Taizu's tent, how could such gifts ever satisfy the soaring ambitions his hegemonic spirit had long fixed upon!
entries.literal: When Yaonian presented drums and banners before Taizu's tent, how could that ever suffice for the lofty gaze of his ambitious, hegemonic spirit!

entries.zh: 厥後交梁聘唐，不憚勞勩。
entries.en: Thereafter they exchanged envoys with Liang and sent embassies to Tang, never shrinking from the effort.
entries.literal: Thereafter they exchanged embassies with Liang and sent missions to Tang, not fearing the toil of the road.

entries.zh: 至於太宗，立晉以要冊禮，入汴而收法物，然後累世之所願欲者，一舉而得之。
entries.en: When it came to Emperor Taizong, he installed Later Jin to demand investiture rites, entered Bianjing and seized the ritual regalia—and thus what generations had long desired was obtained at last in a single stroke.
entries.literal: As for Taizong, he installed Jin to demand investiture rites, entered Bian and collected ritual objects—then what generations had desired was obtained in one stroke.

entries.zh: 太原擅命，力非不敵，席卷法物，先致中京，槊棄山河，不少顧慮，誌可知矣。
entries.en: When Taiyuan acted on its own authority, its strength was hardly inferior—yet it swept up the ritual regalia and sent them first to Zhongjing, casting aside mountains and rivers with scarcely a second thought. Its priorities are plain enough.
entries.literal: Taiyuan acted on its own authority; its strength was not unequal, yet it swept up ritual objects and sent them first to Zhongjing, casting aside mountains and rivers with a spear and scarcely a second thought—its intent may be known.

entries.zh: 於是秦、漢以來帝王文物盡入於遼；
entries.en: Thus the ritual regalia of emperors since Qin and Han all passed into Liao hands;
entries.literal: Thus the ritual regalia of emperors since Qin and Han all entered Liao;

entries.zh: 周、宋按圖更制，乃非故物。
entries.en: while Zhou and Song remade their own according to diagrams—they were no longer the original objects.
entries.literal: Zhou and Song remade them according to diagrams—they were no longer the original objects.

entries.zh: 遼之所重，此其大端，故特著焉。
entries.en: This was the great matter that Liao prized above all, and therefore it is given special record here.
entries.literal: What Liao valued—this was the great point; therefore it is specially recorded.

entries.zh: 天顯四年，太宗幸遼陽府，人皇王備乘輿羽衛以迎。
entries.en: In the fourth year of the Tianxian era (929), Emperor Taizong visited Liaoyang Prefecture, and the Human Emperor King prepared the imperial carriage and feathered guard to welcome him.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Tianxian, Taizong visited Liaoyang Prefecture; the Human Emperor King prepared the imperial carriage and feathered guard to welcome him.

entries.zh: 乾亨五年，聖宗東巡，東京留守具儀衛迎車駕。
entries.en: In the fifth year of the Qianheng era (983), Emperor Shengzong toured the east, and the regent at the Eastern Capital prepared the ceremonial guard to welcome the imperial procession.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Qianheng, Emperor Shengzong toured east; the Eastern Capital regent prepared ceremonial guards to welcome the imperial procession.

entries.zh: 此故渤海儀衛也。
entries.en: This was the ceremonial guard inherited from Bohai.
entries.literal: This was the former Bohai ceremonial guard.

entries.zh: 漢仗
entries.en: Han Regalia
entries.literal: Han paraphernalia

entries.zh: 景宗乾亨五年二月，神柩升辒京車，具鹵簿儀衛。
entries.en: In the second month of the fifth year of the Qianheng era (983), during Emperor Jingzong's reign, the spirit coffin was placed on the encoffining carriage with full outer-guard ceremonial escort.
entries.literal: In the second month of the fifth year of Emperor Jingzong's Qianheng era, the spirit coffin was placed on the encoffining carriage, with full outer-guard ceremonial escort.

entries.zh: 六月，聖宗至上京，留守具法駕迎導。
entries.en: In the sixth month Emperor Shengzong reached the Upper Capital, and the regent prepared the full imperial equipage to welcome and escort him.
entries.literal: In the sixth month, Emperor Shengzong reached the Upper Capital, and the regent prepared the full imperial equipage to welcome and escort him.

entries.zh: 聖宗統和元年，車駕還上京，迎導儀衛如式。
entries.en: In the first year of the Tonghe era (983), the imperial procession returned to the Upper Capital, and the welcoming escort ceremonial guard followed the prescribed form.
entries.literal: In the first year of Emperor Shengzong's Tonghe era, the imperial procession returned to the Upper Capital, and the welcoming escort ceremonial guard followed the prescribed form.

entries.zh: 三年，駕幸上京，留守具儀衛奉迎。
entries.en: In the third year, when the emperor visited the Upper Capital, the regent prepared the ceremonial guard to welcome him.
entries.literal: In the third year, when the emperor visited the Upper Capital, the regent prepared the ceremonial guard to welcome him.

entries.zh: 四年，燕京留守具儀衛導駕入京，上御元和殿，百僚朝賀。
entries.en: In the fourth year, the regent at Yanjing prepared the ceremonial guard to escort the imperial procession into the capital; the emperor ascended the Yuanhe Hall, and the officials offered court congratulation.
entries.literal: In the fourth year, the Yanjing regent prepared ceremonial guards to escort the imperial procession into the capital; the emperor ascended the Yuanhe Hall and the hundred officials offered court congratulation.

entries.zh: 是後，儀衛常事，史不復書。
entries.en: Thereafter, routine matters of ceremonial guard were no longer recorded in the histories.
entries.literal: Thereafter, routine matters of ceremonial guard were no longer recorded in the histories.

entries.zh: 鹵簿儀仗人數馬匹
entries.en: Outer Guard Ceremonial Paraphernalia: Personnel and Horses
entries.literal: Outer guard ceremonial paraphernalia: numbers of personnel and horses

entries.zh: 大同元年正月朔，備法駕至汴，上御崇元殿，受文武百僚朝賀。
entries.en: On the first day of the first month of the first year of Datong (947), with full imperial equipage he reached Bianjing; the emperor ascended the Chongyuan Hall and received the civil and military officials in court congratulation.
entries.literal: On the first day of the first month of the first year of Datong, with full imperial equipage he reached Bian; the emperor ascended the Chongyuan Hall and received the civil and military hundred officials in court congratulation.

entries.zh: 自是日以為常。
entries.en: From then on this became the daily routine.
entries.literal: From then on this became daily routine.

entries.zh: 二月朔，上御崇元殿，備禮受朝賀。
entries.en: On the first day of the second month, the emperor ascended the Chongyuan Hall, performed the full rites, and received court congratulation.
entries.literal: On the first day of the second month, the emperor ascended the Chongyuan Hall, prepared the rites, and received court congratulation.

entries.zh: 三月，將幸中京鎮陽，詔收鹵簿法物，委所司押領先往。
entries.en: In the third month, as he prepared to visit Zhongjing at Zhenyang, an edict ordered the collection of outer-guard ritual regalia and directed the responsible offices to escort them ahead.
entries.literal: In the third month, about to visit Zhongjing Zhenyang, an edict ordered collection of outer guard ritual objects, entrusted to the responsible offices to escort and send ahead.

entries.zh: 未幾鎮陽入漢，鹵簿法物隨世宗歸於上京。
entries.en: Before long Zhenyang fell to the Han, and the outer-guard ritual regalia followed Emperor Shizong back to the Upper Capital.
entries.literal: Before long Zhenyang fell to Han; outer guard ritual objects followed Emperor Shizong back to the Upper Capital.

entries.zh: 四月，皇太弟李胡遣使問軍事，上報曰，朝會起居如禮。
entries.en: In the fourth month, the Imperial Younger Brother Li Hu sent envoys to inquire about military affairs; the emperor reported that court assemblies and daily conduct proceeded according to ritual.
entries.literal: In the fourth month, the Imperial Younger Brother Li Hu sent envoys to inquire about military affairs; the emperor reported that court assemblies and daily conduct proceeded according to ritual.

entries.zh: 是月，太宗崩，世宗即位，鹵簿法物備而不禦。
entries.en: That month Emperor Taizong died and Emperor Shizong succeeded to the throne; the outer-guard ritual regalia were prepared but not employed.
entries.literal: That month Taizong died; Shizong succeeded to the throne—the outer guard ritual objects were prepared but not employed.

entries.zh: 儀衛誌四
entries.en: Ceremonial Guards, Part Four
entries.literal: Ceremonial Guards Treatise, Part Four

entries.en: (Ceremonial Paraphernalia)〉
entries.literal: (Ceremonial Paraphernalia)〉

entries.zh: 初，皇祖勻德實為大叠烈府夷離堇，喜稼穡，善畜牧，相地利以教民耕。
entries.en: In the beginning, the imperial ancestor Junde, as yilijin of the Dadielie Prefecture, took pleasure in farming and excelled at animal husbandry, teaching the people to till the land according to local conditions.
entries.literal: In the beginning, the imperial ancestor Junde served as yilijin of the Dadielie Prefecture. He delighted in farming and was skilled in animal husbandry, assessing the advantages of the land to teach the people to cultivate.

entries.zh: 仲父述瀾為於越，飭國人樹桑麻，習組織。
entries.en: His uncle Shulü, serving as yuyue, directed the people to plant mulberry and hemp and to learn weaving.
entries.literal: His father's younger brother Shulü served as yuyue and ordered the people of the state to plant mulberry and hemp and to learn weaving.

entries.zh: 太祖平諸弟之亂，弭兵輕賦，專意於農。
entries.en: After the Taizu Emperor suppressed his brothers' rebellion, he stilled the armies, lightened taxes, and devoted himself wholly to agriculture.
entries.literal: The Taizu Emperor quelled the rebellion of his younger brothers, stilled the armies and lightened levies, and devoted his mind to agriculture.

entries.zh: 嘗以戶口滋繁，糺轄疏遠，分北大濃兀為二部，程以樹藝，諸部效之。
entries.en: When the population grew and supervisory districts became too remote to manage, he divided the northern Beidanu into two divisions, set planting quotas for each, and the other tribes followed suit.
entries.literal: Once, because the population had grown numerous and supervisory districts were far-flung, he divided the northern Beidanu into two divisions, setting schedules for planting and cultivation, and the various tribes followed his example.

entries.zh: 夫賦稅之制，自太祖任韓延徽，始制國用。
entries.en: The system of levies and taxes dates from the Taizu Emperor's employment of Han Yanhui, who first established state revenues.
entries.literal: As for the system of levies and taxes, from the time the Taizu Emperor employed Han Yanhui, state revenues were first instituted.

entries.zh: 太宗籍五京戶丁以定賦稅，戶丁之數無所於考。
entries.en: The Taizong Emperor registered household males in the Five Capitals to fix levies and taxes, though the exact numbers can no longer be verified.
entries.literal: The Taizong Emperor registered household males of the Five Capitals to fix levies and taxes; the number of household males cannot now be verified.

entries.zh: 聖宗乾亨間，以上京「雲為戶」訾具實饒，善避徭役，遺害貧民，遂勒各戶，凡子錢到本，悉送歸官，與民均差。
entries.en: During the Shengzong Emperor's Qianheng era, at the Supreme Capital the "cloud-as-household" registers were assessed as genuinely wealthy and adept at evading corvée, to the detriment of the poor; the court then ordered that whenever loan interest reached the principal, the full sum be surrendered to the government, and corvée burdens equalized among the people.
entries.literal: During Qianheng of the Shengzong Emperor, at the Supreme Capital the "cloud-as-household" registers were assessed as genuinely wealthy and skilled at evading corvée, to the harm of poor commoners; thereupon each household was compelled—whenever interest on loans reached principal, all was sent back to the government, and corvée was equalized with the people.

entries.zh: 統和中，耶律昭言，西北之眾，每歲農時，一夫偵候，一夫治公田，二夫給糺官之役。
entries.en: During the Tonghe era, Yelü Zhao reported that among the northwestern populace, each farming season one man served as scout, one worked the public fields, and two performed corvée for supervisory officials.
entries.literal: During Tonghe, Yelü Zhao said that among the northwestern populace, each year at farming season one man served as scout, one tended the public fields, and two supplied corvée to the supervisory officials.

entries.zh: 當時沿邊各置屯田戍兵，易田積穀以給軍餉。
entries.en: At that time, garrison-farming troops were posted along the frontiers, tilling fields and stockpiling grain to supply the armies.
entries.literal: At that time along the borders garrison-farming troops were established at each place, exchanging fields and accumulating grain to supply military provisions.

entries.zh: 故太平七年詔，諸屯田在官斛粟不得擅貨，在屯者力耕公田，不輸稅賦，此公田制也。
entries.en: Hence an edict in the seventh year of Taiping: at all garrison farms, government grain might not be sold without authorization; garrison personnel were to work public fields and pay no taxes—this was the public-field system.
entries.literal: Therefore in the seventh year of Taiping an edict said that at all garrison farms the government hu of grain might not be sold without authorization; those at the garrisons were to labor on public fields and pay no levies or taxes—this was the public-field system.

entries.zh: 餘民應募，或治閑田，或治私田，則計畝出粟以賦公上。
entries.en: Other people who answered the call, whether working idle land or private fields, paid grain to the government according to the acreage cultivated.
entries.literal: The remaining people who answered the call, whether cultivating idle land or private fields, then paid grain per mu to the government.

entries.zh: 統和十五年，募民耕灤河曠地，十年始租，此在官閑田制也。
entries.en: In the fifteenth year of Tonghe, commoners were recruited to farm vacant land along the Luan River, with rent due only after ten years—this was the system for idle government land.
entries.literal: In the fifteenth year of Tonghe, the people were recruited to farm the vacant lands along the Luan River; rent began after ten years—this was the system of idle government land.

entries.zh: 又詔山前後未納稅戶，並於密雲、燕樂兩縣，占田置業入稅，此私田制也。
entries.en: Another edict required untaxed households south and north of the mountains to establish holdings in Miyun and Yanyue counties and enter the tax rolls—this was the private-field system.
entries.literal: An edict also ordered households south and north of the mountains that had not yet paid taxes to take up fields and establish holdings in the two counties of Miyun and Yanyue and enter the tax rolls—this was the private-field system.

entries.zh: 各部大臣從上征伐，俘掠人戶，自置郛郭，為頭下軍州。
entries.en: Ministers of the various tribes who followed the emperor on campaign captured households, built their own walled settlements, and established touxia military prefectures.
entries.literal: Ministers of the various tribes who followed the emperor on campaigns captured and carried off households, set up their own walled settlements, and established touxia military prefectures.

entries.zh: 凡市井之賦各歸頭下，惟酒稅赴納上京，此分頭下軍州賦為二等也。
entries.en: All market levies went to the touxia lord; only the wine tax was remitted to the Supreme Capital—thus touxia military prefecture levies were divided into two classes.
entries.literal: All market levies went to the touxia; only the wine tax was delivered to the Supreme Capital—this divided the levies of touxia military prefectures into two grades.

entries.zh: 契丹舊俗，其富以馬，其強以兵。
entries.en: By ancient Khitan custom, wealth was measured in horses and strength in arms.
entries.literal: In the old customs of the Khitan, their wealth lay in horses, their strength in soldiers.

entries.zh: 縱馬於野，弛兵於民。
entries.en: Horses were turned loose on the open steppe, and warriors were dispersed among the clans.
entries.literal: They let horses roam the wilds and released soldiers among the people.

entries.zh: 有事而戰。
entries.en: They fought only when need arose.
entries.literal: When there was business, they fought.

entries.zh: 廣騎介夫，卯命辰集。
entries.en: Cavalry and infantry were mustered far and wide—orders given at dawn, all gathered by mid-morning.
entries.literal: They spread out cavalry and foot soldiers; at the hour of mao they were ordered, and by the hour of chen they assembled.

entries.zh: 馬逐水草，人仰湩酪，挽強射生，以給日用，糗糧芻茭，道在是矣。
entries.en: Horses followed pasture and water; people lived on kumiss and curds, drew powerful bows to hunt game for their daily fare, and carried dried provisions and fodder—the whole economy rested on this.
entries.literal: Horses followed water and grass; people relied on fermented milk and cheese; they drew strong bows and shot game to supply daily needs—dried grain and fodder, the way lay in these.

entries.zh: 以是制勝，所向無前。
entries.en: With this they won their victories and swept all before them.
entries.literal: By this they overcame and won; wherever they went, none stood before them.

entries.zh: 及其有國，內建宗廟朝廷，外置郡縣牧守，制度日增，經費日廣，上下相師，服御浸盛，而食貨之用斯為急矣。
entries.en: Once they possessed a realm, they built ancestral temples and a court within and established commanderies, districts, and prefectural governors without. Institutions multiplied day by day, expenditures swelled, and court and countryside alike grew ever more lavish in dress and display—until the management of finance and supplies became a pressing concern.
entries.literal: When they had a state, within they built ancestral temples and court halls; without they set up commanderies, districts, prefects, and governors. Institutions daily increased, expenditures daily broadened; above and below imitated one another, dress and equipage gradually grew lavish—and the uses of food and goods became urgent.

entries.zh: 於是五京及長春、遼西、平州置鹽鐵、轉運、度支、錢帛諸司，以掌出納。
entries.en: Accordingly, at the Five Capitals and at Changchun, Liaoxi, and Pingzhou, they set up salt-and-iron, transport, expenditure, and coin-and-silk bureaus to oversee revenue and outlay.
entries.literal: Thereupon at the Five Capitals and at Changchun, Liaoxi, and Pingzhou they established salt-and-iron, transport, expenditure, and coin-and-silk offices to manage receipts and disbursements.

entries.zh: 其制數差等雖不可悉，而大要散見舊史。
entries.en: Though the full gradations of these institutions cannot be recovered in every detail, their broad outlines appear here and there in the older annals.
entries.literal: Although the gradations of these institutions cannot all be known in full, the main points are scattered through the old histories.

entries.zh: 若農谷、租賦、鹽鐵、貿易、坑冶、泉幣、群牧，逐類采摭，緝而為篇，以存一代食貸之略。
entries.en: Grain and agriculture, rents and levies, salt and iron, trade, mining and smelting, currency, and herd management are therefore gathered by category and woven into this chapter, to preserve an outline of the dynasty's economic affairs.
entries.literal: As for grain and agriculture, rents and levies, salt and iron, trade, mining and smelting, currency, and herd management—gathering each category in turn and compiling them into a chapter, to preserve an outline of the food and goods of one age.

entries.zh: 聖宗乾亨五年詔曰：「五稼不登，開帑藏而代民稅；
entries.en: In the fifth year of Qianheng, the Shengzong Emperor proclaimed: "When the five grains fail to ripen, open the treasury and pay the people's taxes for them;
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Qianheng of the Shengzong Emperor, an edict said: "When the five grains do not ripen, open the treasury stores and pay taxes on the people's behalf;

entries.zh: 螟蝗為災，罷徭役以恤饑貧。」
entries.en: when caterpillars and locusts bring disaster, suspend corvée labor to relieve the hungry and destitute."
entries.literal: when caterpillars and locusts bring disaster, suspend corvée labor to relieve the hungry and poor."

entries.zh: 統和三年，帝嘗過槁城，見乙室奧隗部下婦人迪輦等黍過熟未獲，遣人助刈。
entries.en: In the third year of Tonghe, passing through Gaocheng, the emperor saw women of the Yishi'ao tribe—Dilian among them—whose millet had passed ripeness yet stood unharvested, and he sent men to help them reap.
entries.literal: In the third year of Tonghe, the emperor once passed through Gaocheng and saw women of the Yishi'ao tribe, Dilian and others, whose millet had overripened yet remained unharvested; he sent men to help reap.

entries.zh: 太師韓德讓言，兵後逋民棄業，禾稼棲畝，募人獲之，以半給獲者。
entries.en: Grand Preceptor Han Derang reported that after the wars, fugitive peasants had abandoned their fields and grain stood ungathered in the furrows; he proposed hiring laborers to harvest it and giving them half the yield.
entries.literal: Grand Preceptor Han Derang said that after the wars, absconding commoners had abandoned their occupations and grain stood ungathered in the fields; he proposed recruiting men to harvest it and giving half to the harvesters.

entries.zh: 政事令室昉亦言，山西諸州給軍興，民力雕敝，田谷多躪於邊兵，請復今年租。
entries.en: Chief Administrator Shi Fang also reported that the western Shanxi prefectures, burdened with military expenses, had exhausted the people and much standing grain had been trampled by frontier troops; he asked that this year's rent be remitted.
entries.literal: Chief Administrator Shi Fang also said that the western Shanxi prefectures, supplying military expenses, had exhausted the people's strength and much grain in the fields had been trampled by frontier troops; he requested remission of this year's rent.

entries.zh: 六年，霜旱，災民饑，詔三司，舊以稅錢折粟，估價不實，其增以利民。
entries.en: In the sixth year, frost and drought brought famine; an edict to the Three Departments noted that tax payments converted to grain had been undervalued and ordered the conversion rate raised for the people's benefit.
entries.literal: In the sixth year, frost and drought afflicted the people with famine; an edict to the Three Departments said that formerly tax money was converted to grain at valuations that were not fair—let them be raised to benefit the people.

entries.zh: 又徙吉避寨居民三百戶於檀、順、薊三州，擇沃壤，給牛、種谷。
entries.en: Three hundred households from Jibi Stockade were also resettled in Tan, Shun, and Ji prefectures on fertile land, with oxen and seed grain provided.
entries.literal: Three hundred households from Jibi Stockade were also relocated to the three prefectures of Tan, Shun, and Ji; fertile soil was chosen for them, and oxen and seed grain were provided.

entries.zh: 十三年，詔諸道置義倉。
entries.en: In the thirteenth year, an edict ordered every circuit to establish charity granaries.
entries.literal: In the thirteenth year, an edict ordered all circuits to establish charity granaries.

entries.zh: 歲秋，社民隨所獲，戶出粟庤倉，社司籍其目。
entries.en: Each autumn, commune members contributed grain in proportion to their harvest, household by household, to fill the granary, and the commune office kept the register.
entries.literal: Each autumn, commune members according to their harvest contributed grain per household to store in the granary, and the commune office registered the accounts.

entries.zh: 歲儉，發以振民。
entries.en: In lean years, the stores were opened to relieve the people.
entries.literal: In lean years, it was distributed to relieve the people.

entries.zh: 十五年，詔免南京舊欠義倉粟，仍禁諸軍官非時畋牧妨農。
entries.en: In the fifteenth year, an edict remitted old debts of charity-granary grain at Nanjing and forbade military officers from hunting or grazing out of season in ways that would harm the crops.
entries.literal: In the fifteenth year, an edict remitted old debts of charity-granary grain owed at Nanjing and also forbade military officers from untimely hunting and herding that would obstruct farming.

entries.zh: 開泰元年，詔曰：「朕惟百姓徭役煩重，則多給工價；
entries.en: In the first year of Kaitai, an edict declared: "When corvée labor weighs too heavily on the people, increase their wages;
entries.literal: In the first year of Kaitai, an edict said: "We consider that when the people's corvée labor is burdensome, then more wages for labor should be given;

entries.zh: 年谷不登，發倉以貸；
entries.en: when the harvest fails, open the granaries and lend grain;
entries.literal: when the year's grain does not ripen, open the granaries to lend;

entries.zh: 田園蕪廢者，則給牛種以助之。」
entries.en: for those whose fields lie fallow, provide oxen and seed to help them restore cultivation."
entries.literal: for those whose fields and gardens lie waste, then give oxen and seed to assist them."

entries.zh: 太平初幸燕，燕民以年豐進土產珍異。
entries.en: Early in the Taiping era, on a visit to Yan, the people of Yan, rejoicing in a bountiful harvest, presented local delicacies and rare produce.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Taiping, when he visited Yan, the people of Yan, because the year was abundant, presented local products and rare delicacies.

entries.zh: 上禮高年，惠鰥寡，賜酺連日。
entries.en: The emperor honored the elderly, showed kindness to widows and orphans, and granted public feasts for days on end.
entries.literal: The emperor honored the aged, showed kindness to widows and the orphaned, and granted feasts for days on end.

entries.zh: 九年，燕地饑，戶部副使王嘉請造船，募習海漕者，移遼東粟餉燕，議者稱道險不便而寢。
entries.en: In the ninth year, famine struck the Yan region; Vice Commissioner Wang Jia of the Household Bureau proposed building ships, recruiting men skilled in sea transport, and shipping grain from Liaodong to feed Yan—but critics declared the route too perilous, and the plan was abandoned.
entries.literal: In the ninth year, when the Yan region suffered famine, Vice Commissioner of the Household Bureau Wang Jia requested building ships, recruiting those skilled in sea transport, and moving grain from Liaodong to supply Yan; debaters said the route was perilous and inconvenient, and the plan was dropped.

entries.zh: 道宗初年，西北雨穀三十里，春州斗粟六錢。
entries.en: Early in the Daozong Emperor's reign, grain reportedly rained across thirty li in the northwest, and at Chunzhou a dou of grain sold for six cash.
entries.literal: In the early years of the Daozong Emperor, in the northwest grain rained for thirty li, and at Chunzhou a dou of grain cost six cash.

entries.zh: 時西蕃多叛，上欲為守禦計，命耶律唐古督耕稼以給西軍。
entries.en: With many western tribes in rebellion, the emperor sought to strengthen frontier defenses and ordered Yelü Tanggu to supervise farming to supply the western armies.
entries.literal: At that time the western tribes rebelled in great numbers; the emperor wished to plan for defense and ordered Yelü Tanggu to supervise farming to supply the western army.

entries.zh: 唐古率眾田臚朐河側，歲登上熟。
entries.en: Tanggu led his men to farm along the Luju River, and year after year they reaped abundant harvests.
entries.literal: Tanggu led the multitude to farm along the Luju River, and each year they achieved abundant harvests.

entries.zh: 移屯鎮州，凡十四稔，積粟數十萬斛，每鬥不過數錢。
entries.en: He then moved his encampment to Zhenzhou; over fourteen harvests he accumulated several hundred thousand hu, and grain sold for only a few cash per dou.
entries.literal: He moved his encampment to Zhenzhou; over fourteen harvests he accumulated several hundred thousand hu of grain, and each dou cost no more than a few cash.

entries.zh: 以馬人望前為南京度支判官，公私兼裕，檢括戶口，用法平恕，乃遷中京度支使。
entries.en: Because Ma Renwang had previously served as judge of the expenditure bureau at Nanjing, where public and private stores alike prospered and he conducted household registration with fair and lenient application of the law, he was then transferred to be expenditure commissioner at the Central Capital.
entries.literal: Because Ma Renwang had previously been judge of the expenditure bureau at Nanjing, public and private affairs were both ample, he inspected and registered households, applied the law with fairness and forbearance, and was then transferred to be expenditure commissioner at the Central Capital.

entries.zh: 視事半歲，積粟十五萬斛，擢左散騎常侍。
entries.en: Within half a year he had accumulated one hundred fifty thousand hu and was promoted to Left Regular Attendant.
entries.literal: After half a year in office he had accumulated one hundred fifty thousand hu of grain and was promoted to Left Regular Attendant.

entries.zh: 遼之農穀至是為盛。
entries.en: Never had Liao's grain production been so abundant.
entries.literal: The grain and agriculture of Liao at this point reached their greatest abundance.

entries.zh: 而東京如咸、信、蘇、復、辰、海、同、銀、烏、遂、春、泰等五十餘城內，沿邊諸州，各有和糴倉，依祖宗法，出陳易新，許民自願假貸，收息二分。
entries.en: Within the Eastern Capital region—in more than fifty cities including Xian, Xin, Su, Fu, Chen, Hai, Tong, Yin, Wu, Sui, Chun, and Tai—and along the frontier prefectures, each locality maintained harmonized-purchase granaries. By ancestral regulation, old grain was released and new grain taken in; voluntary loans to the people were permitted at two percent interest.
entries.literal: Within the Eastern Capital, in more than fifty cities such as Xian, Xin, Su, Fu, Chen, Hai, Tong, Yin, Wu, Sui, Chun, Tai, and the like, and in the frontier prefectures along the borders, each had harmonized-purchase granaries. According to ancestral law, old grain was released and new grain taken in; the people were permitted voluntary loans at two percent interest.

entries.zh: 所在無慮二三十萬碩，雖累兵興，未嘗用乏。
entries.en: Each store held no less than two or three hundred thousand shi; despite repeated warfare, supplies never ran short.
entries.literal: At each place there were no fewer than two or three hundred thousand shi; though warfare arose repeatedly, supplies were never exhausted.

entries.zh: 迨天慶間，金兵大入，盡為所有。
entries.en: By the Tianqing era, when Jin armies swept in, all of it fell into their hands.
entries.literal: By the Tianqing era, when Jin troops entered in force, all was taken by them.

entries.zh: 會天祚播遷，耶律敵烈等逼立梁王雅裏，令群牧人戶運鹽濼倉粟。
entries.en: When the Tianzuo Emperor was driven into exile, Yelü Dilie and others forced the installation of Prince Liang Yali and ordered the herd-management households to transport grain from the Salt Marsh granary.
entries.literal: When the Tianzuo Emperor was driven into exile, Yelü Dilie and others forced the installation of Prince Liang Yali and ordered the herd-management households to transport grain from the Salt Marsh granary.

entries.zh: 人戶侵耗，議籍其產以償。
entries.en: Households suffered losses in transit, and officials proposed registering their property to make them pay compensation.
entries.literal: The households suffered losses in transit, and it was proposed to register their property for compensation.

entries.zh: 雅裏自定其直：粟一車一羊，三車一牛，五車一馬，八車一駝。
entries.en: Yali himself set the compensation rates: one cartload of grain for one sheep, three cartloads for one ox, five for one horse, eight for one camel.
entries.literal: Yali himself set the rates: one cartload of grain for one sheep, three cartloads for one ox, five for one horse, eight for one camel.

entries.zh: 從者曰：「今一羊易粟二斗，尚不可得，此直太輕。」
entries.en: A follower protested: "Today one sheep cannot even buy two dou of grain—these rates are far too lenient."
entries.literal: A follower said: "Today one sheep cannot even be exchanged for two dou of grain—this rate is far too light."

entries.zh: 雅里曰：「民有則我有。
entries.en: Yali replied: "What the people possess, I possess.
entries.literal: Yali said: "When the people have, then I have.

entries.zh: 若令盡償，眾何以堪？」
entries.en: If I demand full compensation, how can the people endure it?"
entries.literal: If I order full compensation, how can the multitude bear it?"

entries.zh: 事雖無及，然使天未絕遼，斯言亦足以收人心矣。
entries.en: Though nothing came of it in the end, had Heaven not abandoned Liao, this saying alone would have been enough to win the people's hearts.
entries.literal: Though the matter came to nothing in the end, yet had Heaven not cut off Liao, this saying alone would have been enough to win people's hearts.

entries.zh: 食貨志上
entries.en: Finance and Economics, Part One
entries.literal: Treatise on Food and Goods, Part One

entries.zh: 征商之法，則自太祖置羊城於炭山北，起榷務以通諸道市易。
entries.en: Merchant taxation began under Taizu, when he established the Sheep Market north of Coal Mountain and opened monopoly trading offices to facilitate commerce along the highways.
entries.literal: As for the method of levying merchants, it began when Taizu established Yang Market north of Tan Mountain and set up monopoly offices to connect market exchange on all routes.

entries.zh: 太宗得燕，置南京，城北有市，百物山偫，命有司治其征；
entries.en: After Taizong seized the Yan region, he made it the Southern Capital. A market north of the city wall teemed with goods heaped high as a hill, and he charged the authorities with collecting duties on it;
entries.literal: When Taizong obtained Yan, he established the Southern Capital; north of the city wall there was a market with goods piled like a mountain, and he ordered the relevant offices to administer its levies;

entries.zh: 余四京及它州縣貨產懋遷之地，置亦如之。
entries.en: The same arrangement was made at the other four capitals and in prefectures and counties wherever goods were plentiful and trade was active.
entries.literal: The remaining four capitals and other prefectures and counties where goods were abundant and commerce flourished were set up the same way.

entries.zh: 東平郡城中置看樓，分南、北市，禺中交易市北，午漏下交易市南。
entries.en: In the Dongping commandery seat they built a watchtower and divided trade between southern and northern markets: business in the northern market ran through the Wei hour (9–11 a.m.), and in the southern market after midday.
entries.literal: In the seat of Dongping Commandery a lookout tower was erected, dividing South and North markets; at the center of the Wei hour trading was in the North Market, after the midday clepsydra mark trading was in the South Market.

entries.zh: 雄州、高昌、渤海亦立互市，以通南宋西北諸部、高麗之貨，故女直以金、帛、布、蜜、蠟諸藥材，及鐵離、靺鞨、於厥等部以蛤珠、青鼠、貂鼠、膠魚之皮、牛羊駝馬、毳罽等物，來易於遼者，道路繦屬。
entries.en: Mutual markets were also opened at Xiongzhou, Gaochang, and Bohai to channel goods from the northwestern tribes beyond Song territory and from Korea. Jurchen traders brought gold, textiles, cloth, honey, wax, and medicinal products; tribes such as Tieli, Mohe, and Yujue brought clam pearls, blue voles, sable, fish glue and hides, livestock, and felts to exchange in Liao territory, and the trade routes were unbroken with caravans.
entries.literal: Xiong, Gaochang, and Bohai also established mutual markets to connect goods from the northwestern tribes of Song to the south and from Korea; therefore the Jurchen brought gold, silk, cloth, honey, wax, and various medicinals, and the Tieli, Mohe, Yujue, and other tribes brought clam pearls, blue mice, sable mice, fish glue skins, oxen, sheep, camels, horses, felt rugs, and such things to trade with Liao—the roads were continuous with traders.

entries.zh: 聖宗統和初，燕京留守司言，民艱食，請弛居庸關稅，以通山西糴易。
entries.en: Early in Emperor Shengzong's Tonghe reign, the Yanjing military commission reported that the populace lacked grain and asked that customs duties at Juyong Pass be eased so that Shanxi grain could be brought in.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Shengzong's Tonghe era, the Yanjing garrison headquarters reported that the people had difficulty obtaining food and requested that the Juyong Pass duties be relaxed to open Shanxi grain purchase and trade.

entries.zh: 又令有司諭諸行宮，布帛短狹不中尺度者，不鬻於市。
entries.en: He further directed officials to notify all traveling palaces that cloth and silk below standard length or width was not to be offered for sale.
entries.literal: He also ordered the relevant offices to instruct the various traveling palaces that cloth and silk that were short, narrow, and not up to measure were not to be sold in the market.

entries.zh: 明年，詔以南、北府市場人少，宜率當部車百乘赴集。
entries.en: The following year an edict noted sparse attendance at the southern and northern palace markets and ordered each responsible tribe to muster a hundred cart-loads of goods for the fairs.
entries.literal: The next year, an edict stated that because the South and North Palace markets had few people, the appropriate tribes should be led with a hundred cart loads each to assemble there.

entries.zh: 開奇峰路以通易州貿易。
entries.en: The Qifeng route was opened to facilitate trade with Yizhou.
entries.literal: The Qifeng Road was opened to connect trade with Yizhou.

entries.zh: 二十三年，振武軍及保州並置榷場。
entries.en: In year 23, monopoly border markets were established at Zhenwu Army and Baozhou.
entries.literal: In the twenty-third year, Zhenwu Army and Baozhou both established monopoly markets.

entries.zh: 時北院大王耶律室魯以俸羊多闕，部人貧乏，請以羸老之羊及皮毛易南中之絹，上下為便。
entries.en: At that time Yelü Shilu, grandee of the Northern Chancellery, reported that stipend sheep were chronically short and his tribesmen were impoverished; he asked to exchange old or weak sheep and hides for southern silk, which met with approval at every level.
entries.literal: At that time the Northern Chancellery Grandee Yelü Shilu, because salary sheep were often lacking and his tribesmen were poor, requested to exchange lean old sheep and fur for silk from the south; above and below found it convenient.

entries.zh: 至天祚之亂，賦斂既重，交易法壞，財日匱而民日困矣。
entries.en: By the turmoil of Emperor Tianzuo's reign, levies had grown crushing, commercial regulations had collapsed, and both treasury and populace sank ever deeper into want.
entries.literal: By the disorders of Tianzuo, exactions had become heavy, trade laws were broken, wealth daily exhausted and the people daily distressed.

entries.zh: 鹽筴之法，則自太祖以所得漢民數多，即八部中分古漢城別為一部治之。
entries.en: The salt monopoly dated from Taizu, who, having absorbed large numbers of Han subjects, carved Ancient Han City out of the eight tribes as a separate administrative division for their governance.
entries.literal: As for the salt monopoly law, it began when Taizu, because the Han subjects he had acquired were numerous, separated Ancient Han City from among the eight tribes as a separate tribe to administer them.

entries.zh: 城在炭山南，有鹽池之利，即後魏滑鹽縣也，八部皆取食之。
entries.en: The settlement lay south of Coal Mountain near productive salt ponds—the site of the Later Wei county of Huayan—and all eight tribes drew their salt from it.
entries.literal: The city was south of Tan Mountain, with the benefit of salt ponds; it was the Later Wei county of Huayan, and all eight tribes took salt there to eat.

entries.zh: 及征幽、薊還，次於鶴剌濼，命取鹽給軍。
entries.en: On returning from the You and Ji campaign, he encamped at Hela Marsh and ordered salt drawn from the ponds to supply the army.
entries.literal: When he returned from campaigning in You and Ji, he halted at Hela Marsh and ordered salt taken to supply the army.

entries.zh: 自後濼中鹽益多，上下足用。
entries.en: Thereafter salt from the marshlands grew plentiful, and court and camp alike had enough.
entries.literal: From then on salt in the marsh increased, and above and below had enough to use.

entries.zh: 會同初，太宗有大造於晉，晉獻十六州地，而瀛、莫在焉，始得河間煮海之利，置榷鹽院於香河縣，於是燕、雲迤北暫食滄鹽。
entries.en: Early in the Huitong era, after Taizong's decisive aid to the Later Jin, the Jin ceded the Sixteen Prefectures—including Ying and Mo—and Liao gained access to Hejian's sea-salt industry. A salt monopoly bureau was set up in Xianghe county, and for a time the Yan and Yun regions northward relied on Cangzhou salt.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Huitong, Taizong had great merit toward Jin; Jin presented the sixteen prefectures, and Ying and Mo were among them; he first obtained the benefit of boiling sea salt at Hejian and established a salt monopoly office in Xianghe County; thus Yan and Yun northward for a time ate Cangzhou salt.

entries.zh: 一時產鹽之地如渤海、鎮城、海陽、豐州、陽洛城、廣濟湖等處，五京計司各以其地領之。
entries.en: Salt-producing districts such as Bohai, Zhencheng, Haiyang, Fengzhou, Yangluo city, and Guangji Lake were placed under the respective accounting offices of the five capitals.
entries.literal: For a time salt-producing places such as Bohai, Zhencheng, Haiyang, Fengzhou, Yangluo City, Guangji Lake, and the like were each administered by the accounting offices of the five capitals according to their territories.

entries.zh: 其煎取之制，歲出之額，不可得而詳矣。
entries.en: The methods of boiling and extraction and the annual output quotas cannot be recovered in detail.
entries.literal: The regulations for boiling and extracting, and the annual output quotas, cannot be obtained in detail.

entries.zh: 坑冶，則自太祖始並室韋，其地產銅、鐵、金、銀，其人善作銅鐵器。
entries.en: Mining and smelting began when Taizu first annexed the Shiwei, whose lands yielded copper, iron, gold, and silver and whose people were skilled metalworkers.
entries.literal: As for mines and smelting, it began when Taizu first annexed the Shiwei; their land produced copper, iron, gold, and silver, and their people were skilled at making copper and iron implements.

entries.zh: 又有曷術部者多鐵，「曷術」，國語鐵也。
entries.en: The Heshu tribe also possessed abundant iron deposits—"heshu" being the Khitan word for iron.
entries.literal: There was also the Heshu tribe, which had much iron; "heshu" in the national language means iron.

entries.zh: 部置三冶：曰柳濕河，曰三黜古斯，曰手山。
entries.en: Three smelting works were established for the tribe: at Liushi River, San Chugusi, and Shoushan.
entries.literal: The tribe set up three smelteries: called Liushi River, San Chugusi, and Shoushan.

entries.zh: 神冊初，平渤海，得廣州，本渤海鐵利府，改曰鐵利州，地亦多鐵。
entries.en: Early in the Shence era, after the conquest of Bohai, Guangzhou was taken—it had been Bohai's Tieli prefecture and was renamed Tieli prefecture, another iron-rich district.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Shence, Bohai was pacified and Guangzhou was obtained; it had originally been Bohai's Tieli prefecture, renamed Tieli Prefecture, and the land also had much iron.

entries.zh: 東平縣本漢襄平縣故地，產鐵礦，置采煉者三百戶，隨賦供納。
entries.en: Dongping county occupied the site of the Han dynasty's Xiangping county. Iron ore was mined there, and three hundred smelting households were registered to deliver tribute as assessed.
entries.literal: Dongping County was on the old site of Han Xiangping County; it produced iron ore, and three hundred households of miners and smelters were established to supply tribute according to levies.

entries.zh: 以諸坑冶多在國東，故東京置戶部司，長春州置錢帛司。
entries.en: Because most mines lay in the eastern territories, a Households Bureau was set up at the Eastern Capital and a Money and Textiles Bureau at Changchun prefecture.
entries.literal: Because the various mines and smelteries were mostly in the east of the state, the Eastern Capital established a Households Bureau and Changchun Prefecture established a Money and Textiles Bureau.

entries.zh: 太祖征幽、薊，師還，次山麓，得銀、鐵礦，命置冶。
entries.en: On returning from the You and Ji campaign, Taizu encamped in the foothills, discovered silver and iron deposits, and ordered smelting works built.
entries.literal: When Taizu campaigned in You and Ji and the army returned, he halted at the mountain foothills, obtained silver and iron ore, and ordered smelteries established.

entries.zh: 聖宗太平間，於潢河北陰山及遼河之源，各得金、銀礦，興冶采煉。
